standard.title: Characters and events across contexts
standard.description: discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts in literature by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature from diverse contexts (AC9E2LE01). They have not yet compared how the same character type (e.g. the wolf) or story element is portrayed differently across texts from different cultural contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss characters, events and settings in different contexts in literature by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Same story, different tellings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how the same story or character type is told differently by different authors, identifying variations in characters, events and settings.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two versions of the same story or story type and identify at least two differences in how characters, events or settings are presented.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how different wide-ranging authors tell the same story — identifying variations in character portrayal, setting and events; discuss how the same character type (e.g. the wolf) is portrayed differently in different versions.
wider: Compare a traditional story told by a First Nations Australian author with a mainstream version, discussing what is similar and what reflects different relationships with Country, family and community
Discuss why different authors might portray the same character type differently — connecting authorial choice to cultural perspective and purpose

response_modes.reason: Students easily accept a single version of a story as 'the real one'. Seeing multiple tellings — especially cross-cultural ones — reveals that character, setting and event are constructed choices, not fixed facts. This is a conceptual shift that multiple examples are needed to secure.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The explicitly named First Nations Australian literature context offers one of the most educationally significant width opportunities in Y3 Literature. Characters' relationships with Country/Place and families are structurally different from Western narrative conventions — this is rich and important territory for building cultural understanding through literature.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two specific differences in character, event or setting across two versions of a story
Student discusses one reason why the versions might differ — not just listing differences

nodes.label: Australian settings in literature
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how Australian settings are portrayed in stories and identify distinctive features of how Australian places and environments are represented.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how one Australian setting is portrayed in a story and discuss at least one feature of how the setting is described.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how Australian settings are portrayed in stories — discussing distinctive landscape, environment and cultural features — and compare with how settings from other cultural contexts are presented.
wider: Compare how First Nations Australian authors portray Country/Place as a living, relational entity with how non-Indigenous Australian authors portray the same or similar landscapes
Discuss how the portrayal of Australian settings has changed across different time periods in children's literature
success_criteria: Student identifies a specific Australian setting in a text and names at least one feature of how it is described
Student discusses what the setting contributes to the story — not just where it is
